nodes.label: doctor exit code contract
nodes.rationale: 0 all pass, 1 at least one FAIL, 2 warnings only; CI and make demo both refuse to proceed on 1.

nodes.label: doctor.py check contract
nodes.rationale: The single highest-leverage file for the clone experience: it answers 'why can't I run this?' before the user has to read a stack trace. Every FAIL carries a runnable command or a document anchor, and credentials are reported set/unset/expired with no value ever printed.

nodes.label: The three-tier contract
nodes.rationale: Higher tiers are additive, never prerequisites; tier 0 is the promise and must work offline on a clean clone with no .env edits.

nodes.label: Secret handling rules
nodes.rationale: Never log a token, not even truncated; the refresh-token secret keeps a short version retention policy because old versions are expired credentials.

nodes.label: No-secrets-in-output guarantee (spike)
nodes.rationale: Proven by test, not by inspection: the report must not contain the token, not even a truncated prefix. The token file is also opened 0600 rather than chmod'd afterwards, because write-then-chmod leaves a window in which it is world-readable.

nodes.label: Injected-probe check design
nodes.rationale: Every check is a pure function returning a CheckResult with its environment probe injected as a parameter, so the whole suite runs with no Docker, no network, and no gcloud.

nodes.label: Leak-canary secret test
nodes.rationale: An earlier draft asserted the substring SECRET never appears, which false-positives immediately because the variable is named GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET and printing the name is the point; the invariant is that the value never appears, so values carry a canary that cannot collide with any variable name.

nodes.label: Memgraph Lab service
nodes.rationale: Lab is where a cloner inspects the demo graph, which is most of the 'wow'.

nodes.label: Local memgraph-mage service
nodes.rationale: Tag must match Phase 1's Terraform GCE VM image or MAGE procedure availability differs between local and deployed, and a nightly job that passes locally fails there.

nodes.label: Local Postgres 15 service
nodes.rationale: Postgres major version matches Cloud SQL (15) so local testing is evidence about production.

nodes.label: LLM configuration seam
nodes.rationale: One protocol (chat_json/embed) owns every backend so no module constructs its own client; temperature is pinned at 0.0 for extraction; the privacy claim is restated as 'never leaves our GCP tenancy' rather than overstated.

nodes.label: Four LLM backends behind one protocol
nodes.norm_label: four llm backends behind one protocol
nodes.rationale: Adds gemini and fake while keeping llm_client.py's protocol unchanged and its position as the only module that constructs an LLM client.

nodes.label: Local compose stack design
nodes.rationale: The API runs on the host rather than in compose so the edit-reload loop stays fast during Phases 3-8; a cloner never runs a second command to see the dashboard.

nodes.label: Reproducibility risks
nodes.rationale: Biggest: the local Memgraph image drifting from the VM image, mitigated by the same pinned tag in compose and Terraform and asserted by doctor at tier 2.

nodes.label: 768-dimensional embedding invariant
nodes.rationale: Both Memgraph vector indexes are configured for 768, so every backend must emit 768 dims or both indexes need migrating.

nodes.label: Pinned image tags taken from v5
nodes.norm_label: pinned image tags taken from v5
nodes.rationale: Tags are taken from v5's live-validated compose rather than guessed; the API deliberately does not run in compose so the edit-reload loop stays fast during Phases 3-8.

nodes.label: Bug 4: literal 'null' strings from the LLM
nodes.norm_label: bug 4: literal 'null' strings from the llm
nodes.rationale: Gemma emits the string 'null' rather than a JSON null, and a non-empty string is truthy so falsiness checks do not catch it. Verify Gemini too - do not assume immunity.

nodes.label: Unignoring docker-compose.local.yml
nodes.rationale: The *.local.* scratch rule would swallow the compose file, which is a committed first-class file, so an explicit negation is added first - before the task that creates it.

nodes.label: Hash-keyed fixture replay
nodes.rationale: Fixtures are keyed by a hash of system prompt + user content + temperature so a prompt edit produces a loud miss that raises rather than falling through to a default; record_fixtures.py regenerates in one command.

nodes.label: Meet transcripts via Workspace Events
nodes.rationale: Transcription is an admin-enabled Workspace feature; if unavailable the Source seam lets sources/meet.py be a no-op, exactly as v5's meet_ingest.pull_and_stage degrades.

nodes.label: Meet: reachable vs transcripts-present
nodes.rationale: An HTTP 200 with zero conference records means the API is reachable but the tenant has no transcripts - a different answer from 'the call failed' - and conflating them would misreport a Phase 0.5 exit criterion.

nodes.label: graphify maintenance discipline
nodes.rationale: Commit GRAPH_REPORT.md and graph.json but never graphify-out/cache/; v5 tracked ~180 cache files by accident.

nodes.label: Standing exit criterion (spec)
nodes.rationale: What prevents the retrofit; the local stack is exercised continuously rather than rotting.

nodes.label: LM Studio becomes one of two LLM backends (§2.3)
nodes.norm_label: lm studio becomes one of two llm backends (§2.3)

nodes.label: Ephemeral-port loopback callback server
nodes.rationale: Binding 127.0.0.1:0 removes the 'port 8888 is busy' failure mode v5's refresh_gcal_token.py works around, since Desktop OAuth clients accept any loopback port. State is validated to prevent CSRF and the access log is silenced because it would echo the authorization code.

nodes.label: BigQuery as the staging layer — rejected
nodes.norm_label: bigquery as the staging layer — rejected

nodes.label: GKE Autopilot from day one — deferred
nodes.norm_label: gke autopilot from day one — deferred

nodes.label: Spanner Graph instead of Memgraph — rejected
nodes.norm_label: spanner graph instead of memgraph — rejected

nodes.label: The four minimal OAuth scopes
nodes.rationale: Request the minimum; every additional scope makes an admin allowlist request harder to approve, and all four are read-only which helps when asking for approval.

nodes.label: Loopback redirect and prompt=consent
nodes.rationale: The out-of-band flow is deprecated, and without an explicit prompt=consent Google may not return a refresh token on a repeat authorisation.

nodes.label: Deferred to v2: dev_agent and action_agent
nodes.norm_label: deferred to v2: dev_agent and action_agent
nodes.rationale: The pipeline has to be solid first, but the provenance schema ships in v1 anyway because provenance cannot be backfilled - a merge before the schema exists is lost forever.

nodes.label: Bug 9: Leiden over-fragmentation
nodes.rationale: Community detection collapsed to all-singletons; check v5's git history for the fix.

nodes.label: Order of porting
nodes.rationale: Pure modules first for an early green suite, then I/O, LLM seam, connectors, pipeline, intelligence, API. Do not start with the connectors - they depend on Phase 0.5's outcome.

nodes.label: Personal-then-Onix deployment context
nodes.rationale: Infrastructure project and data-source Workspace account are deliberately different, which makes portability a first-class design constraint rather than a later concern.

nodes.label: Property graph schema
nodes.rationale: Sourced from the live v5 graph rather than v5's own docs, because the live graph proved more accurate. Edge vocabulary is deliberately aligned with Matteo's engagement ontology so the graph is legible to anyone who knows it.

nodes.label: meeting-notes-gcp v6
nodes.rationale: v6 is a deliberate fresh-repo port of v5, not a rewrite: the deployment target moved from a MacBook to GCP, so Airbyte and in-process scheduling could not survive, while Memgraph+MAGE, FastAPI, the extraction prompts and the test suite are assets worth carrying across.

nodes.label: Repository layout
nodes.rationale: jobs/ and api/ are entrypoints only; a job file past ~50 lines means the logic belongs in the meeting_notes package.

nodes.label: v1-v6 version lineage
nodes.rationale: v3 and v4/v5 repos are read-only reference so that no local-first or Airbyte assumption leaks back in by accident.

nodes.label: Migration to the Onix project
nodes.rationale: An Internal client removes expiry, the test-user list and verification all at once; everything else is unchanged, which is the whole point of portability as a design constraint.

nodes.label: StagedRecord normalisation question
nodes.rationale: v5's four Raw* models overlap; since v6 owns every connector they normalise to one row shape with a per-source adapter. Decide it before writing db.py - it affects every connector.

nodes.label: db.py dual-mode connection
nodes.rationale: Decided now rather than during Phase 3 because a data-layer shape settled after the connectors exist is far more expensive to change.

nodes.label: Intent-to-skill map
nodes.rationale: Non-Claude-Code agents get an explicit intent table because they do not read the plugin skill listing.

nodes.label: Coding conventions
nodes.rationale: Tests must run with no live GCP, database, or LLM; a test requiring live credentials is a broken test. v5 achieved this for 363 tests and the property must not regress.

nodes.label: Live v5 graph inventory
nodes.rationale: Inspected 2026-08-13, more accurate than v5's own docs. 61 of 84 meetings are standups and AgentRun is inflated by bug 2, so any PageRank or community result from it is distorted.

nodes.label: v5 to v6 port map
nodes.rationale: Lift / Adapt / Rewrite / Drop per module, so every carried-over file is consciously chosen.

nodes.label: Module boundaries
nodes.rationale: These boundaries held perfectly in v5, so they are carried unchanged: SQL only in db.py, generic Cypher only in graph_client.py, MAGE CALL only in graph_algorithms.py, Jira REST only in jira_client.py, os.environ only in config.py, LLM clients only in llm_client.py.

nodes.label: Person.tracked governance gate
nodes.rationale: Aggregates are the default and naming individuals is opt-in, so every per-person analytic must filter on tracked = true.

nodes.label: Never pass event= to structlog
nodes.rationale: event= collides with structlog's reserved message field and raises TypeError at call time - this was a real production 500 in v5.

nodes.label: Lowercased Topic MERGE key
nodes.rationale: Raw case fragmented single topics across multiple nodes in v5 and silently understated every insight query.

nodes.label: Deterministic uuid5_id node ids
nodes.rationale: Deterministic ids make reprocessing idempotent under MERGE; writer/reader id drift is a known past bug class that cost real debugging time twice.

nodes.label: OAuth user type follows the project/account split
nodes.norm_label: oauth user type follows the project/account split
nodes.rationale: A GCP project and a Google account are independent, but where the project lives determines whether the client can be Internal (no verification, no expiry) or only External.

nodes.label: The 7-day refresh token problem
nodes.rationale: External + Testing issues refresh tokens that expire after exactly 7 days; Gmail's restricted scopes make publishing to Production require verification plus a third-party security assessment. Expiry must be loud - a pipeline that silently stops for four days is worse than one that pages you weekly.

nodes.label: Workspace admin third-party app block
nodes.rationale: If 'unconfigured third-party apps' is set to block, an OAuth client from an unknown personal project cannot access Onix data at all no matter how correct the code is - a hard stop, and the reason Phase 0.5 exists. Workspace trust and Google verification are two separate gates.

nodes.label: Bug 1: ASSIGNED_TO never forms
nodes.rationale: The Cypher matches Person by email but the extractor emits display names, so the live edge count is zero. Fix: resolve action.owner through person_resolver before the write.

nodes.label: Bug 2: get_active_run resume loop
nodes.rationale: A successful run parks at SHIPPED, which was not in the terminal set, so every poll re-resumed it and produced 61 AgentRun nodes for one ticket.

nodes.label: Bug 8: sync_jira_issue always returned True
nodes.rationale: Returned success even when zero nodes matched, making the counters meaningless.

nodes.label: Bug 6: provenance id drift
nodes.rationale: Ids derived in one place and re-derived differently in another meant reads never found what writes created. Bit the project twice.

nodes.label: Bug 3: structlog reserved kwarg
nodes.rationale: log.info(..., event=event) raises TypeError at call time - a real HTTP 500 on /webhook/github that every test missed by calling the handler directly.

nodes.label: Bug 10: test-stub pollution
nodes.rationale: Test files stubbed optional dependencies behind 'if mod_name not in sys.modules', so whichever test ran first won for the whole session; conftest.py's _REAL_HTTPX fix is load-bearing.

nodes.label: Bug 7: get_ticket_provenance missing c.message
nodes.rationale: Forward and reverse traversals returned different shapes; test that their RETURN shapes match.

nodes.label: Bug 5: Topic case fragmentation
nodes.rationale: Raw-case MERGE keys made 'Migration' and 'migration' two nodes with a colliding uuid5 id.

nodes.label: Non-goals of the reproducibility design
nodes.rationale: Terraform will not create the OAuth consent screen or client, no Workspace admin approval can be automated, make demo never writes to a real Jira, and it stays single-tenant.

nodes.label: Problem: a stranger can run nothing
nodes.norm_label: problem: a stranger can run nothing
nodes.rationale: Each credential is a wall, and the first is hit before a single line of the project's actual value is visible.

nodes.label: Realistic sample meeting corpus
nodes.rationale: Not cosmetic: seeding a skewed corpus would bake v5's 73%-standup distortion into every cloner's first impression. Seeding must be idempotent.

nodes.label: Airbyte residue to delete
nodes.rationale: v5's db.py carries scar tissue from Airbyte writing hash-suffixed table names; processed_gmail_ids stays because it survives a full re-sync independently of Airbyte.

nodes.label: APScheduler removed → Cloud Scheduler + Cloud Run Jobs (§2.2)
nodes.norm_label: apscheduler removed → cloud scheduler + cloud run jobs (§2.2)

nodes.label: Hand-rolled OAuth over httpx
nodes.rationale: Three reasons over google_auth_oauthlib.InstalledAppFlow: CLAUDE.md mandates httpx.AsyncClient and the Google client libraries are synchronous httplib2; the exchange/refresh helpers are reused verbatim by Phase 5's refresh_tokens job; and the script must import nothing from meeting_notes/ because that package is empty until Phase 2.

nodes.label: make sync-down
nodes.rationale: gcloud sql export sql to the GCS bucket, a google_compute_snapshot of the Memgraph disk, then terraform destroy scoped to the ephemeral tier only. A skipped or interrupted sync-down is a silent cost leak, so doctor should grow a tier-2 check that warns when the ephemeral tier is up with no active session.

nodes.label: sync-down session end (~3 min)
nodes.rationale: Backs up, verifies the backup, then destroys. It will not destroy anything until it has confirmed both backups exist — a failed export leaves the tier up and tells you so rather than silently discarding a month of work. Between sessions the billable tier costs $0.

nodes.label: ADR-017 — Phase 1 validated live: the sync lifecycle works, and costs ~11 minutes to start
nodes.norm_label: adr-017 — phase 1 validated live: the sync lifecycle works, and costs ~11 minutes to start
nodes.rationale: ADR-016 was decided on price-list arithmetic and never run. A full cycle against real infrastructure returned both marker records with their original timestamps, proving data survives the gap. Declaring Phase 1 done on a green terraform apply was rejected — it would have shipped all four bugs, none of which appear until the second half of a cycle; skipping marker records was rejected because a destroy/apply of empty resources proves only that Terraform is deterministic.

nodes.label: Backup-before-destroy guarantee
nodes.rationale: sync-down must confirm both the Cloud SQL export and the disk snapshot before terraform destroy runs. The property held in production unrehearsed: when the snapshot step failed, terraform destroy correctly never ran, the ephemeral tier stayed up, and the error said so.

nodes.label: Bug 4 — gcloud storage ls exits 1 on an empty prefix
nodes.norm_label: bug 4 — gcloud storage ls exits 1 on an empty prefix
nodes.rationale: It exits 1 with 'matched no objects', not 0 with empty output. The unit test mocked exit 0, so it passed while the first real sync-up failed — the mock certified the bug it was meant to catch. gcloud compute disks snapshot likewise needs an explicit --zone.

nodes.label: Bug 2 — cloudresourcemanager and iam APIs missing from required list
nodes.norm_label: bug 2 — cloudresourcemanager and iam apis missing from required list
nodes.rationale: Service-account creation succeeded without iam.googleapis.com; the subsequent read of the same resource 403'd — a failure mode that only shows up one step later than the operation that should have failed.

nodes.label: Cloud SQL provisioning is the sync-up long pole
nodes.norm_label: cloud sql provisioning is the sync-up long pole
nodes.rationale: The eleven minutes is entirely Cloud SQL instance provisioning; the Memgraph VM serves Bolt in about two minutes and is not the problem. Because the long pole is precisely located, the fix is scoped if cadence ever changes: keep Cloud SQL running and tear down only the VM (~$13/mo), or move staging to something with a faster cold start.

nodes.label: A fake-backend fixture miss raises
nodes.rationale: Fixtures are keyed by a hash of (system prompt + user content + temperature), so a prompt edit changes the hash and produces a loud immediate failure rather than a silently-wrong extraction. It never falls through to None, a default, or an empty extraction. scripts/record_fixtures.py regenerates against a real backend so a deliberate prompt change is one command.

nodes.label: Four bugs found by running the full cycle that review missed
nodes.norm_label: four bugs found by running the full cycle that review missed
nodes.rationale: Every one was a wrong assumption about how a Google API behaves, and none appears until the second half of a full cycle (commit 7972f9a). Bug 4 is the instructive one: a mock encoded an assumption about a tool's behaviour, the assumption was wrong, and the test therefore certified the bug. Every fix now carries a test that would have caught it, and mocks match observed CLI behaviour rather than expected behaviour.

nodes.label: Marker-record proof of data survival across teardown
nodes.norm_label: marker-record proof of data survival across teardown
nodes.rationale: Markers written to both stores before sync-down returned with their original timestamps after the next sync-up (2026-08-20T02:19:19 in Memgraph, 2026-08-20T02:21:04 in Postgres), with Cloud SQL and Compute both reporting 'Listed 0 items' while torn down. 'destroy then apply worked' proves only that Terraform is deterministic and says nothing about the data.

nodes.label: Measured sync-up duration (~11–12 minutes)
nodes.rationale: Taken from Cloud SQL operation logs and the GCE serial console, not estimated: Cloud SQL instance creation 11m05s cold / 10m46s restoring, Memgraph VM boot to serving Bolt ~2m13s, full sync-up ~11–12 min and full sync-down ~3 min (export+verify+snapshot ~25s, Cloud SQL deletion ~1m50s). A fair trade for $0 idle at a monthly cadence; intolerable at a daily one.

nodes.label: Orphan export from a partially completed sync-down
nodes.norm_label: orphan export from a partially completed sync-down
nodes.rationale: One sync-down failed at the snapshot step (missing --zone) after the export had already succeeded, leaving meeting-memory-20260820t022231z.sql.gz in the backup bucket with no matching snapshot. The bucket's 90-day lifecycle rule reclaims it, so it is untidy rather than a leak — but a partially completed sync-down is now a known and observed state, not a theoretical one.

nodes.label: Phase 1 outcome — sync lifecycle proven end to end against real GCP
nodes.norm_label: phase 1 outcome — sync lifecycle proven end to end against real gcp
nodes.rationale: A full cycle ran: durable apply → sync-up → markers written to both stores → sync-down → verified 'Listed 0 items' and $0 → sync-up → both markers returned with their original timestamps. Data survives the gap. sync-up ~11–12 min, sync-down ~3; running it found four bugs review had missed, and the backup-before-destroy guarantee held unrehearsed.

nodes.label: Measured sync timings in the tier-2 walkthrough
nodes.norm_label: measured sync timings in the tier-2 walkthrough
nodes.rationale: Budget about eleven minutes for sync-up and three for sync-down — measured, not estimated (ADR-017). Cloud SQL and the Memgraph VM together run about $58/month if left up, which is why they exist only during a session.

nodes.label: Standing exit criterion — Phases 1 through 9
nodes.rationale: A clean clone still passes make doctor, make demo is green from Phase 6, example tfvars stay committed and real ones gitignored, and graphify . --update is run with the report and graph.json committed but never cache/. This is what stops reproducibility becoming a retrofit at Phase 9, and it makes the local stack the continuously exercised test harness for Phases 3–8.

nodes.label: make doctor — tier-aware preflight
nodes.rationale: Names every gap and gives a runnable fix for each; that is its whole job. Secrets are reported set/unset/expired, never valued. At TIER=2 it also warns before the refresh token dies and reports the ephemeral tier as UP with its burn rate if you forgot sync-down.

nodes.label: IAP tunnel to Memgraph Bolt
nodes.rationale: Memgraph's Bolt port is never exposed publicly; gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel meeting-notes-memgraph 7687 --local-host-port=localhost:7687 --zone=$GCP_ZONE is the way in.

nodes.label: sync-up session start (~11 min)
nodes.rationale: Creates the billable resources, restores the last backup, and runs doctor. Nearly all of it is Cloud SQL provisioning; the Memgraph VM serves Bolt after roughly two minutes, so the graph is usable well before the database is. Start a session before you need it.

nodes.label: ADR-013 — Three-tier reproducibility contract with a permanently manual OAuth console step
nodes.norm_label: adr-013 — three-tier reproducibility contract with a permanently manual oauth console step
nodes.rationale: Nothing in the repo could be run by anyone who is not Shubham, and the first wall (a GCP project with billing) is hit before any of the project's value is visible. Three additive tiers let a stranger evaluate offline in ten minutes. GCP-deploy-only was rejected as the problem itself; local-demo-only leaves the GCP-native headline unclonable. Cost: a docker-compose path production never uses, and the risk a green tier 0 is misread as evidence about tier 2.

nodes.label: ADR-015 — db.py selects its connection mode on configuration
nodes.norm_label: adr-015 — db.py selects its connection mode on configuration
nodes.rationale: Tier 0 runs against a plain Postgres container and tier 2 against Cloud SQL through the Python connector; left undecided the question surfaces during Phase 3 after db.py exists. Branching on CLOUD_SQL_CONNECTION_NAME keeps one query path so local testing is evidence about production. Cloud-SQL-connector-only would force every cloner to run a credentialed proxy, defeating tier 0; two modules would put SQL outside db.py.

nodes.label: Phase 0.6 — Reproducibility skeleton
nodes.rationale: Builds only the scaffolding that stands on its own today — doctor, docker-compose.local.yml, .env.example, example tfvars, SETUP.md, Makefile — with fake/gemini backends, the sample corpus, dual-mode db.py and a working make demo attributed to the phases that own them. No check may emit a secret value, asserted by a test with a canary that cannot collide with a variable name.

nodes.label: Tier 0 — local, no credentials
nodes.rationale: make demo over sample meetings with LLM_BACKEND=fake replaying recorded fixtures — no API key, no network, deterministic, and the resulting graph is real because it is built by the real pipeline. Tier 0 passing says the logic is sound and says nothing about your cloud setup. make demo deliberately fails with an explanation until Phases 6 and 8 land, rather than pretending to succeed.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting — Cloud SQL Proxy v2 not found in PATH
nodes.norm_label: troubleshooting — cloud sql proxy v2 not found in path
nodes.rationale: gcloud sql connect needs a component not installed by default: gcloud components install cloud-sql-proxy. Connecting to the instance's public IP directly with psql or asyncpg will hang, and that is by design — there are no authorized networks, so the only routes in are the IAM-authenticated Cloud SQL connector or the proxy.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting — local port already in use
nodes.norm_label: troubleshooting — local port already in use
nodes.rationale: Something already listens on 5432, 7687, 7444, or 8080. If it is this project's own stack that is fine; otherwise stop it or run make demo-down.

nodes.label: 768-dimensional embeddings in every backend
nodes.rationale: Both Memgraph vector indexes are configured for 768, and Vertex text-embedding-005 outputs 768 by default — so vector_memory needs an endpoint change, not a reindex (verified 2026-08-13). fake included.

nodes.label: llm_client.py single-protocol backend seam
nodes.rationale: One unchanged protocol (chat_json, embed) selected by LLM_BACKEND=vertex|gemini|lmstudio|fake, keeping llm_client.py the only module that constructs an LLM client.

nodes.label: Durable-tier one-time apply
nodes.rationale: make tf-bootstrap creates the state bucket once, then tf-init/tf-apply MODULE=durable brings up VPC, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager, service accounts, Pub/Sub, the backup bucket and the budget alert — cents per month, and it stays up. Run make doctor TIER=2 before spending money.

nodes.label: ADR-002 — Vertex AI Gemini as default LLM behind a swappable seam
nodes.norm_label: adr-002 — vertex ai gemini as default llm behind a swappable seam
nodes.rationale: v5's 'extraction is always local LM Studio' rule served a privacy claim and a cost constraint, neither of which survives on GCP. One protocol with LLM_BACKEND selection costs about one file and keeps the free local path; the privacy claim is restated as 'never leaves our GCP tenancy'. Self-hosting Gemma on GKE was rejected — a GPU node would be the largest line item to serve a model worse at structured JSON.

nodes.label: ADR-014 — A fake LLM backend replaying fixtures, and a gemini backend for tier 1
nodes.norm_label: adr-014 — a fake llm backend replaying fixtures, and a gemini backend for tier 1
nodes.rationale: Neither vertex (needs billing) nor lmstudio (needs a multi-gigabyte download and a capable Mac) can deliver tier 0's no-credentials promise. Gemini-only was rejected because one env var is not zero, is not offline, and free-tier rate limits make a first run flaky; LM-Studio-only is a far steeper wall than 'put in your credentials'. Four backends is more surface to keep working and fixtures must be re-recorded on deliberate prompt changes.

nodes.label: Tier 1 — real LLM
nodes.rationale: One free AI Studio key (no GCP project, no billing) swaps replayed fixtures for genuine extraction and embeddings. lmstudio is the local-model alternative; embeddings must be 768-dimensional in every backend because the Memgraph vector indexes are built for 768.

nodes.label: Tier 2 — deploy to your own GCP
nodes.norm_label: tier 2 — deploy to your own gcp
nodes.rationale: The real thing, and the only tier with an unavoidable manual step. The durable tier is applied once and costs cents per month; real .tfvars and .backend.hcl are gitignored because they carry project ids, with committed *.example.* alongside so required variables stay discoverable.

nodes.label: OAuth console step accepted as permanently manual
nodes.norm_label: oauth console step accepted as permanently manual
nodes.rationale: Google exposes no usable API for an External-type consent screen or a Desktop client with restricted Gmail scopes; google_iap_brand and google_iap_client cover neither case. Terraform will never create it. Detected and explained rather than papered over, because pretending otherwise produces a terraform apply that fails confusingly.

nodes.label: The part nobody can automate — OAuth console setup
nodes.norm_label: the part nobody can automate — oauth console setup
nodes.rationale: Google exposes no API for creating an OAuth consent screen or a Desktop client with restricted Gmail scopes, so it is hand-work in the console, once, and make doctor TIER=2 tells you if it is not done. The console splits it across separate Audience and Data Access pages rather than one linear wizard, which is why older single-'OAuth consent screen' guides look different.
nodes.source_location: Tier 2 — The part nobody can automate

nodes.label: Troubleshooting — Error 401 invalid_client during consent
nodes.rationale: The client ID in .env does not match a real OAuth client — usually a typo, or the client was created in a different project than the one you are pointed at. Newly created clients can also take a few minutes to propagate.

nodes.label: 7-day refresh token expiry (External + Testing OAuth client)
nodes.norm_label: 7-day refresh token expiry (external + testing oauth client)
nodes.rationale: Gmail's restricted scopes make Production verification (plus a third-party security assessment) non-viable, so the client stays External + Testing and refresh tokens die weekly. jobs/refresh_tokens.py automates access-token refresh but cannot extend a refresh token's own expiry; only re-consent or an Internal client in the Onix project does. At a monthly sync cadence re-consent is every session, so it belongs in the sync-up walkthrough rather than a troubleshooting footnote.

nodes.label: ADR-009 — Personal GCP project now, Onix Workspace data throughout
nodes.norm_label: adr-009 — personal gcp project now, onix workspace data throughout
nodes.rationale: Three consequences accepted knowingly: the OAuth client must be External + Testing, so refresh tokens expire every 7 days (Gmail restricted scopes make Production verification non-viable); the Onix admin might block unverified apps outright, which is why Phase 0.5 exists as a gate; and Onix meeting content sits in a personal project, mitigated by own-mailbox-only and short raw-table retention.

nodes.label: ADR-012 — Phase 0.5 auth spike passed, no admin allowlisting needed
nodes.norm_label: adr-012 — phase 0.5 auth spike passed, no admin allowlisting needed
nodes.rationale: A factual outcome, not a design choice — no alternatives rejected. Gmail, Calendar and Meet all returned real records on the first consent attempt; ADR-009's worst-case admin-block risk did not materialise. Meet transcription is enabled on the Onix tenant, so Phase 5 can build the transcript path as first-class rather than assuming the no-op fallback.

nodes.label: Phase 0.5 — Auth spike (DONE 2026-08-19)
nodes.rationale: Gated every later phase: if the Onix Workspace admin blocked unverified third-party apps the entire ingestion design changes and everything built before finding out is wasted. Passed on the first attempt with no admin allowlisting; Meet transcription is enabled, so sources/meet.py can be first-class in Phase 5.

nodes.label: Phase 10 — Onix migration
nodes.rationale: A new Internal-type OAuth client removes the 7-day expiry and the verification requirement entirely; the personal project is then decommissioned and its data destroyed.

nodes.label: Phase 9 — Hardening and demo
nodes.rationale: Backup and restore must be rehearsed by actually restoring, and the demo must run end to end without a laptop in the loop, unattended for a week beyond OAuth re-consent.

nodes.label: The 7-day clock in the tier-2 runbook
nodes.norm_label: the 7-day clock in the tier-2 runbook
nodes.rationale: Expect to re-consent every session: any gap longer than a week means sync-up's doctor run reports the token expired, which is normal at this cadence rather than a fault. make auth-spike ARGS=--reconsent renews it; the permanent fix is an Internal client in an Onix-owned project.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting — consent succeeds but API calls 403
nodes.norm_label: troubleshooting — consent succeeds but api calls 403
nodes.rationale: The scopes on the consent screen do not match the four the code requests, or the Workspace admin has restricted third-party app access.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting — worked yesterday, fails today
nodes.rationale: It is the 7-day refresh token. Run make auth-spike ARGS=--reconsent.

nodes.label: Ephemeral resource tier (Cloud SQL instance + Memgraph VM and disk)
nodes.norm_label: ephemeral resource tier (cloud sql instance + memgraph vm and disk)
nodes.rationale: The only always-on-priced resources; created at the start of a sync session and torn down at the end, so idle cost is a guaranteed $0.

nodes.label: v2 — Deferred scope
nodes.rationale: dev_agent ports only with bug #2 fixed (the SHIPPED resume loop that created 61 AgentRun nodes for one ticket); action_agent is re-evaluated rather than ported because it sits on the Airbyte Agents SDK; plus users.watch push notifications and the GKE Autopilot migration.

nodes.label: ADR-003 — Keep Memgraph; reject Spanner Graph
nodes.norm_label: adr-003 — keep memgraph; reject spanner graph
nodes.rationale: Spanner Graph would maximise the GCP-native claim but GQL is not openCypher, so graph_client.py becomes a rewrite; there is no MAGE (so every graph algorithm — the project's actual differentiator — is reimplemented), no in-engine vector index, and no MCP server. The price of keeping Memgraph is owning a stateful VM and its backups.

nodes.label: ADR-004 — Memgraph on a GCE VM first, GKE later
nodes.norm_label: adr-004 — memgraph on a gce vm first, gke later
nodes.rationale: Memgraph needs persistent storage and always-on availability so Cloud Run is out. A GCE VM is meaningfully cheaper during the personal-billing phase. Deliberately reversible: the application connects over bolt://host:7687 either way and no application code can tell the difference.

nodes.label: Phase 7 — Graph intelligence
nodes.rationale: Check v5's git history for the Leiden over-fragmentation fix before enabling community detection, and seed a realistic meeting-type mix before drawing any conclusion from PageRank — the v5 graph is 73% standups and its algorithm output is distorted accordingly.

nodes.label: Bug 3 — gcloud sql export writes as the instance's own service account
nodes.norm_label: bug 3 — gcloud sql export writes as the instance's own service account
nodes.rationale: Not the calling identity. That account is regenerated on every instance creation, so the bucket grant must live in the ephemeral module bound to service_account_email_address — a static durable-tier binding would go stale on the first teardown.

nodes.label: Durable resource tier (bucket, secrets, registry, Pub/Sub, IAM, budget alert)
nodes.norm_label: durable resource tier (bucket, secrets, registry, pub/sub, iam, budget alert)
nodes.rationale: Created once and never destroyed by the normal lifecycle; all cheap-to-free while idle, and the place where data lives between sessions.

nodes.label: make sync-up
nodes.rationale: terraform apply recreating Cloud SQL (importing the latest GCS export if one exists) and the Memgraph VM (disk from source_snapshot = latest), then make doctor TIER=2 — which is expected to report the OAuth refresh token as expired at this cadence, a runbook step rather than a bug to chase.

nodes.label: ADR-011 — config.py is the only reader of os.environ
nodes.norm_label: adr-011 — config.py is the only reader of os.environ
nodes.rationale: v5 read os.environ in a dozen modules including call-time lambdas, which enabled a real test-isolation bug where a test silently depended on an ambient variable being unset. A single typed settings object surfaces configuration errors at startup and lets tests override an object instead of mutating global environment state.

nodes.label: ADR-016 — Ephemeral compute, durable storage: the system is up only when syncing
nodes.norm_label: adr-016 — ephemeral compute, durable storage: the system is up only when syncing
nodes.rationale: Verified against the live Cloud Billing Catalog API, e2-medium is ~$40/mo and db-f1-micro ~$13/mo if left running — irrelevant if the resources do not exist between sessions. Stopping was rejected because Cloud SQL auto-restarts after ~7 days, silently resuming the bill. Half-measures (tear down only Memgraph) and smaller always-on tiers do not earn back their complexity for a system touched a few hours a month.

nodes.label: Phase 1 — Terraform foundation (DONE 2026-08-20)
nodes.rationale: Everything in code, no console clicks. Exit criteria deliberately demanded that sync-down then sync-up reproduce the environment with data intact, proven by a marker record rather than assumed from the export/import commands succeeding. Prices had to be checked against current GCP rates and the budget alert set before the first apply — ARCHITECTURE.md's estimates were unverified.

nodes.label: Phase 2 — Pure core
nodes.rationale: The no-I/O modules port nearly unchanged and give a green suite early. The StagedRecord question must be settled as an ADR before db.py exists — deciding it after the connectors exist is much more expensive.

nodes.label: Bug 1 — google provider needs user_project_override + billing_project
nodes.norm_label: bug 1 — google provider needs user_project_override + billing_project
nodes.rationale: Without both settings, billingbudgets.googleapis.com rejects user ADC credentials outright.

nodes.label: Stopping instead of destroying does not work
nodes.norm_label: stopping instead of destroying does not work
nodes.rationale: gcloud sql instances patch --activation-policy=NEVER halts Cloud SQL billing, but Google auto-restarts a stopped instance after ~7 days for maintenance, silently resuming the bill mid-gap. A stopped GCE VM has no equivalent forced restart, so 'stop everything' is not a single reliable pattern; destroying is the only mode with a guaranteed $0 idle for both.

nodes.label: Billing, not code, was Phase 1's real blocker
nodes.norm_label: billing, not code, was phase 1's real blocker
nodes.rationale: Two personal billing accounts were closed and 'not in good standing'. The working setup is a billing account owned by work.shubham.gaur.x@gmail.com with roles/billing.user granted to shubham.gaur.x@gmail.com, which the project links to — $300 trial credit, 90 days.
nodes.source_location: Phase 1 — Note for the next phase

nodes.label: Troubleshooting — Terraform 'requires a quota project'
nodes.rationale: Application Default Credentials are missing or pointed at the wrong account; fix with gcloud auth application-default login.

nodes.label: Provenance schema ships in v1, writers in v2
nodes.norm_label: provenance schema ships in v1, writers in v2
nodes.rationale: Ticket, PullRequest, AgentRun, Commit, FileChange, Blocker and their edges are created in v1's schema setup and /webhook/github exists in v1, because provenance cannot be backfilled.

nodes.label: ADR-001 — Fresh repository, deliberate port
nodes.rationale: Clone-and-refactor would inherit v5's local-first, Airbyte-shaped assumptions invisibly; a full rewrite would throw away extraction prompts, Cypher, and live-debugged tests. A fresh repo forces each carried file to be consciously chosen, at the cost of re-establishing the test suite phase by phase.

nodes.label: ADR-005 — Replace APScheduler with Cloud Scheduler + Cloud Run Jobs
nodes.norm_label: adr-005 — replace apscheduler with cloud scheduler + cloud run jobs
nodes.rationale: v5's ten APScheduler jobs would force min-instances=1 on Cloud Run — paying for an always-on container while keeping APScheduler's failure mode where a tick exception is logged and forgotten with no retry and no alert. The largest structural difference between v5 and v6; it introduces overlapping executions, addressed by ADR-006.

nodes.label: ADR-006 — Claim rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
nodes.norm_label: adr-006 — claim rows with select ... for update skip locked
nodes.rationale: v5 ran exactly one container so WHERE processed = false was safe; Cloud Run Jobs can overlap. Combined with deterministic uuid5_id ids and mandatory MERGE, reprocessing is idempotent. Jira issue creation stays the one non-idempotent side effect and must be gated on ActionItem.jira_key IS NULL inside the claiming transaction.

nodes.label: ADR-007 — Build our own connectors; remove Airbyte
nodes.norm_label: adr-007 — build our own connectors; remove airbyte
nodes.rationale: v5's bore/ngrok tunnel existed only because the destination Postgres was local. Owning connector code buys no tunnel, no third-party dependency, no per-connector cost, and full control of sync cadence, at the price of owning watermarks and OAuth token lifecycle. Precedent exists in-house: v5's meet_ingest.py is hand-written and the simplest ingestion path there.

nodes.label: ADR-008 — Defer dev_agent and action_agent to v2, ship provenance schema in v1
nodes.norm_label: adr-008 — defer dev_agent and action_agent to v2, ship provenance schema in v1
nodes.rationale: Porting both agents alongside the pipeline would roughly double v1 and delay anything demo-able. But provenance cannot be backfilled — a merge before the schema exists is lost forever — so shipping the schema early costs almost nothing and preserves the option. action_agent is built on the Airbyte Agents SDK, the exact dependency v6 walks away from.

nodes.label: ADR-010 — Collapse the three duplicated pipeline paths into one
nodes.norm_label: adr-010 — collapse the three duplicated pipeline paths into one
nodes.rationale: v5's graph_builder.py had three ~90% identical functions with a nine-call memory-enrichment block copy-pasted verbatim three times; drift between them is invisible. One pipeline.process(record, adapter) makes a fifth source an adapter rather than a fourth copy, at slight indirection cost.

nodes.label: Phase 3 — Data layer
nodes.rationale: Staging schema as a migration rather than a 5-minute heartbeat; every trace of Airbyte table-discovery deleted; the six Cypher queries v5 leaked into main.py moved into graph_client.py. Concurrent drain executions must be proven to claim disjoint batches by test, not assumed.

nodes.label: Phase 4 — LLM seam
nodes.rationale: Keep v5's system prompt verbatim — it is tuned — and swap only the client, retaining _is_null_like and _loads_lenient. Vertex model names are env vars, never literals, and text-embedding-005's 768 dimensions must be verified against the live API rather than relied on. Transport errors retry; JSON parse failures do not.

nodes.label: Phase 5 — Connectors
nodes.rationale: The only genuinely new code in the project. A deliberately expired token must produce a visible alert rather than silent failure, and re-running a connector must stage no duplicates.

nodes.label: Phase 6 — Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Fixes v5 bug #1 by resolving action.owner through person_resolver so ASSIGNED_TO actually forms — verified with a Cypher count, not by reading the code. Confidence gating must route a low-confidence item to needs_review with no ticket, and dedup must not open a second ticket for a repeated action item.

nodes.label: Phase 8 — API and dashboard
nodes.rationale: Every v5 endpoint with zero APScheduler, single-file dashboard with no build step, webhooks public but HMAC-verified. /graph/insights/influential must respect the Person.tracked gate — it is the governance promise — and every route needs an httpx.ASGITransport test driving the real ASGI app.
